The Universe That Reproduces

Could Black Holes Be the Children of Other Universes?

Article

Introduction

Some physicists have explored the possibility that black holes could create new universes. Physicist Lee Smolin took this idea further: perhaps universes reproduce, slightly change, and go through something similar to natural selection.

This is a serious scientific hypothesis, but it has not been proven.

Before you begin

Warm-up

  1. What do you already know about black holes and the Big Bang?

  2. Have you ever thought about whether our universe could have a 'parent' universe?

  3. What does the term 'natural selection' mean to you, and can it apply outside biology?

Reading

Part 1: What if our universe had a parent?

We normally imagine the Big Bang as the absolute beginning. About 13.8 billion years ago, our observable universe was extremely hot and dense. Space expanded, matter formed, stars appeared, planets developed, and eventually life became possible.

But this leaves one enormous question: Why did the Big Bang happen at all? And another: Was it truly the beginning, or did something exist before it? One strange possibility is that our universe was born inside something else.

Imagine a black hole existing in an older universe. From the outside, matter falls into the black hole and seems to disappear behind the event horizon.

But perhaps the story does not end there. Some speculative theories of quantum gravity suggest that the extreme collapse inside a black hole might not continue forever into an infinitely dense singularity.

Instead, the collapse could somehow “bounce.” That bounce might create a new expanding region of spacetime. From inside that new region, the event might look surprisingly similar to a Big Bang.

This leads to the first crazy possibility: A black hole in one universe could become the beginning of another universe.

Reading

Part 2: Why black holes are important

A black hole forms when enough matter becomes concentrated in a small region. Its gravity becomes so strong that beyond the event horizon, even light cannot escape. According to classical general relativity, matter falling deep inside eventually approaches a singularity—a region where the equations predict extreme curvature and our normal description of spacetime breaks down.

But physicists do not usually interpret this as proof that nature literally contains an infinitely dense point. It may instead mean: Our current theory has reached its limit. General relativity describes gravity extremely well. Quantum mechanics describes very small systems extremely well. Inside a black hole, however, we need to understand both extreme gravity and quantum physics at the same time.

We still do not have a complete theory of quantum gravity. Because of this, we do not know with confidence what happens at the deepest interior of a black hole. And that uncertainty leaves room for ideas such as a bounce or a baby universe.

Reading

Part 3: A universe hidden behind the black hole

Now imagine falling toward a black hole. From the perspective of someone far away, you cross the event horizon and can never communicate back. But suppose the interior geometry continues into a new expanding region.

That new region might become separated from the original universe. People in the parent universe would simply see: a black hole. But hypothetical observers inside the new region might see: an expanding universe.

This is why these hypothetical regions are sometimes called baby universes. The parent and child might remain connected in a mathematical description of spacetime, or the child universe might effectively “pinch off” and become causally separate. If it became fully separate, inhabitants of the child universe might have no way of discovering their parent directly.

This produces an extraordinary possibility: Every black hole we see might hide an enormous expanding universe on the other side. A small object from our perspective could therefore contain an entire cosmos from another perspective.

Part 4: Lee Smolin's strange next step

The idea becomes much stranger with physicist Lee Smolin. Smolin asked: If black holes create new universes, what happens if the new universes are slightly different from their parents?

Suppose a universe has physical constants. These constants control things such as:

• particle masses

• forces

• nuclear reactions

• gravity

• star formation

Now imagine that when a black hole produces a child universe, these values change slightly. Not completely. Just a little. The child therefore resembles the parent but is not exactly identical.

This gives us something surprisingly similar to biological reproduction.

Biology

Parent organism → child → slightly different genes

Cosmology

Parent universe → black hole → child universe → slightly different physical constants

Once reproduction and variation exist, another possibility appears: selection.

Reading

Part 5: Natural selection — but for universes

Consider biological evolution. Some organisms have traits that help them reproduce. Those organisms produce more children. Their traits therefore become more common in future generations.

Smolin asked whether something similar could happen to universes. Imagine two kinds of universe.

Universe A

Its physical laws produce very few stars. Very few stars means very few black holes. It produces: 10 child universes

Universe B

Its physical laws are excellent for creating large stars. Many large stars eventually collapse into black holes. It produces: 1,000,000 child universes

If the child universes inherit approximately similar physical laws, then after many generations, universes like B become much more common. Not because somebody designed them. Not because they are trying to survive. Simply because: Universes that make more black holes make more universes.

Smolin called this idea Cosmological Natural Selection.

Part 6: The incredible consequence: physical laws may have evolved

Normally we ask: “Why do the laws of physics have these particular values?” For example, why does gravity have its exact strength? Why do particles have their particular masses? Why do nuclear reactions work in a way that allows stars to exist?

Usually these values are treated as basic facts of our universe. Smolin's hypothesis suggests a radically different possibility: Perhaps these values have a history. They may be similar to biological traits.

Imagine changing one physical constant slightly. Perhaps stars become unstable. Then fewer black holes form. That universe produces fewer descendants. Another set of constants may produce enormous numbers of long-lived stars and black holes. Those universes reproduce more successfully. After many cosmic generations, the population of universes could become concentrated around laws that are especially good at producing black holes.

In this picture, the laws of nature that look “special” may not have been chosen. They may have been selected. That is an enormous conceptual change.

Instead of asking: “Who designed these constants?” or: “Did we simply get lucky?” we could ask: “Did these constants evolve?”

Part 7: Where do humans fit into this?

This produces another fascinating idea. Our universe happens to have laws that allow:

• stable stars

• heavy chemical elements

• carbon

• planets

• complex chemistry

• life

This is sometimes called the fine-tuning problem. Why does the universe seem so suitable for complexity? One answer is the anthropic principle: We observe a universe compatible with life because otherwise we would not exist to observe it.

But cosmological natural selection gives a different possibility. Perhaps the universe was not selected for life. Perhaps it was selected for black holes. Life might simply be a side effect. Why? The conditions that help create black holes also require complex astrophysics: stars → nuclear fusion → heavy elements → supernovae → black holes

Those same stars also create the carbon, oxygen, iron, and other elements needed for planets and life. So perhaps: The universe was not “designed” for us at all. We may simply benefit from physical conditions that were good at producing stars and black holes. Life could be an accidental passenger inside a universe optimized for something completely different.

Part 8: A cosmic family tree

If this process happened repeatedly, reality might contain a gigantic family tree of universes. Imagine:

Universe 1 ↓ 1,000 black holes ↓ 1,000 child universes ↓ each produces thousands of black holes ↓ millions of grandchildren universes

After enough generations, the number could become enormous. Some branches would die quickly because their physics produces almost no black holes. Other branches would reproduce extremely successfully. The multiverse would therefore not be a random collection of universes. It could have:

• ancestry

• generations

• inheritance

• variation

• selection

In other words: The multiverse could have a history. Just as every human belongs to an enormous biological family tree, our universe might belong to a cosmic family tree stretching through realities we can never directly observe.

Part 9: Black holes become something completely different

This hypothesis also changes the meaning of a black hole. Normally, black holes represent destruction. Matter falls inside. Stars disappear. Information seems trapped. They are often described as cosmic graves.

But under the baby-universe idea, a black hole could simultaneously be: death from one perspective

and: birth from another. A collapsing star in our universe could produce a Big Bang somewhere else. This creates a beautiful symmetry:

Star dies → black hole forms → new universe begins → new stars form → new black holes form → more universes begin

Destruction becomes reproduction. The objects we call the “dead ends” of spacetime could actually be its reproductive organs. That is perhaps the wildest part of the idea.

Part 10: Could our Big Bang have been a black hole?

Now reverse the idea. If black holes in our universe create baby universes, perhaps our universe is also a baby universe. Then somewhere in a parent cosmos, billions of years—or perhaps a completely different kind of time—ago, a star or other enormous structure may have collapsed.

A black hole formed. From the parent's perspective: matter disappeared behind an event horizon. From our perspective: spacetime began expanding. Our Big Bang could therefore be the inside view of something that looked like a black hole from outside. If true, asking: “What happened before the Big Bang?”

might be similar to asking: “What happened in the parent universe?” But there is a serious difficulty. The causal structure of a black hole may prevent information from the parent universe from reaching us. We might literally be unable to look backward beyond our own cosmic birth.

Part 11: The biggest problem: where is the evidence?

This is where we must separate fascinating physics from established physics. We know black holes exist. We have strong astronomical evidence for them, including gravitational-wave detections and images of black-hole environments.

But we do not know that black holes create universes. That requires physics beyond our currently confirmed understanding of black-hole interiors. Smolin tried to make his theory scientifically useful by proposing a prediction. If universes have evolved to maximize black-hole production, then the physical constants in our universe should be close to values that produce unusually many black holes.

If scientists could change one constant slightly in a theoretical model and reliably produce more black holes, that could challenge the hypothesis. This makes the proposal more interesting than simply saying: “Maybe other universes exist.” It tries to connect the idea to things we can calculate about our universe.

However, scientists continue to debate whether these tests are strong enough and whether the biological natural-selection analogy really works.

Part 12: Why the idea remains scientifically interesting

Cosmological natural selection is not the standard accepted explanation of our universe. But the broader questions behind it remain active in theoretical physics. Researchers continue to study:

• black-hole interiors

• quantum gravity

• singularity removal

• cosmological bounces

• wormholes

• baby universes

Even in 2026, theoretical papers continue exploring mathematical models where baby universes can emerge from black-hole interiors or early-universe processes. This does not mean Smolin's full theory has been confirmed. It means the deeper question—

Can one region of spacetime produce another expanding universe? —remains a serious theoretical question.

Part 13: The deepest philosophical idea

The most powerful part of this hypothesis may not even be the black holes. It is the idea that we might be thinking about the laws of nature incorrectly. We usually imagine: laws first → universe follows laws

But cosmological natural selection suggests: universes reproduce → laws vary → some laws reproduce more successfully

Now the laws themselves become part of history. This is similar to what Darwin did to biology. Before Darwin, species seemed fixed. A tiger was simply a tiger. After Darwin, a tiger became the current result of a historical process.

Smolin asks whether we could make the same conceptual change in physics. Perhaps an electron's mass or gravity's strength is not simply: “the number nature chose.” Perhaps it is: the surviving result of a cosmic evolutionary history. Whether this is true or not, that question completely changes how we think about the universe.

Lesson audio

Introduction

Some physicists have explored the possibility that black holes could create new universes.

Physicist Lee Smolin took this idea further: perhaps universes reproduce, slightly change, and go through something similar to natural selection.

This is a serious scientific hypothesis, but it has not been proven.

Reading

Part 1: What if our universe had a parent?

We normally imagine the Big Bang as the absolute beginning.

About 13.8 billion years ago, our observable universe was extremely hot and dense.

Space expanded, matter formed, stars appeared, planets developed, and eventually life became possible.

But this leaves one enormous question: Why did the Big Bang happen at all?

And another: Was it truly the beginning, or did something exist before it?

One strange possibility is that our universe was born inside something else.

Imagine a black hole existing in an older universe.

From the outside, matter falls into the black hole and seems to disappear behind the event horizon.

But perhaps the story does not end there.

Some speculative theories of quantum gravity suggest that the extreme collapse inside a black hole might not continue forever into an infinitely dense singularity.

Instead, the collapse could somehow “bounce.”

That bounce might create a new expanding region of spacetime.

From inside that new region, the event might look surprisingly similar to a Big Bang.

This leads to the first crazy possibility: A black hole in one universe could become the beginning of another universe.

Reading

Part 2: Why black holes are important

A black hole forms when enough matter becomes concentrated in a small region.

Its gravity becomes so strong that beyond the event horizon, even light cannot escape.

According to classical general relativity, matter falling deep inside eventually approaches a singularity—a region where the equations predict extreme curvature and our normal description of spacetime breaks down.

But physicists do not usually interpret this as proof that nature literally contains an infinitely dense point.

It may instead mean: Our current theory has reached its limit.

General relativity describes gravity extremely well.

Quantum mechanics describes very small systems extremely well.

Inside a black hole, however, we need to understand both extreme gravity and quantum physics at the same time.

We still do not have a complete theory of quantum gravity.

Because of this, we do not know with confidence what happens at the deepest interior of a black hole.

And that uncertainty leaves room for ideas such as a bounce or a baby universe.

Reading

Part 3: A universe hidden behind the black hole

Now imagine falling toward a black hole.

From the perspective of someone far away, you cross the event horizon and can never communicate back.

But suppose the interior geometry continues into a new expanding region.

That new region might become separated from the original universe.

People in the parent universe would simply see: a black hole.

But hypothetical observers inside the new region might see: an expanding universe.

This is why these hypothetical regions are sometimes called baby universes.

The parent and child might remain connected in a mathematical description of spacetime, or the child universe might effectively “pinch off” and become causally separate.

If it became fully separate, inhabitants of the child universe might have no way of discovering their parent directly.

This produces an extraordinary possibility: Every black hole we see might hide an enormous expanding universe on the other side.

A small object from our perspective could therefore contain an entire cosmos from another perspective.

Reading

Part 4: Lee Smolin's strange next step

The idea becomes much stranger with physicist Lee Smolin.

Smolin asked: If black holes create new universes, what happens if the new universes are slightly different from their parents?

Suppose a universe has physical constants.

These constants control things such as: • particle masses • forces • nuclear reactions • gravity • star formation Now imagine that when a black hole produces a child universe, these values change slightly.

Not completely.

Just a little.

The child therefore resembles the parent but is not exactly identical.

This gives us something surprisingly similar to biological reproduction.

Biology Parent organism → child → slightly different genes Cosmology Parent universe → black hole → child universe → slightly different physical constants Once reproduction and variation exist, another possibility appears: selection.

Reading

Part 5: Natural selection — but for universes

Consider biological evolution.

Some organisms have traits that help them reproduce.

Those organisms produce more children.

Their traits therefore become more common in future generations.

Smolin asked whether something similar could happen to universes.

Imagine two kinds of universe.

Universe A Its physical laws produce very few stars.

Very few stars means very few black holes.

It produces: 10 child universes Universe B Its physical laws are excellent for creating large stars.

Many large stars eventually collapse into black holes.

It produces: 1,000,000 child universes If the child universes inherit approximately similar physical laws, then after many generations, universes like B become much more common.

Not because somebody designed them.

Not because they are trying to survive.

Simply because: Universes that make more black holes make more universes.

Smolin called this idea Cosmological Natural Selection.

Reading

Part 6: The incredible consequence: physical laws may have evolved

Normally we ask: “Why do the laws of physics have these particular values?”

For example, why does gravity have its exact strength?

Why do particles have their particular masses?

Why do nuclear reactions work in a way that allows stars to exist?

Usually these values are treated as basic facts of our universe.

Smolin's hypothesis suggests a radically different possibility: Perhaps these values have a history.

They may be similar to biological traits.

Imagine changing one physical constant slightly.

Perhaps stars become unstable.

Then fewer black holes form.

That universe produces fewer descendants.

Another set of constants may produce enormous numbers of long-lived stars and black holes.

Those universes reproduce more successfully.

After many cosmic generations, the population of universes could become concentrated around laws that are especially good at producing black holes.

In this picture, the laws of nature that look “special” may not have been chosen.

They may have been selected.

That is an enormous conceptual change.

Instead of asking: “Who designed these constants?”

or: “Did we simply get lucky?”

we could ask: “Did these constants evolve?”

Reading

Part 7: Where do humans fit into this?

This produces another fascinating idea.

Our universe happens to have laws that allow: • stable stars • heavy chemical elements • carbon • planets • complex chemistry • life This is sometimes called the fine-tuning problem.

Why does the universe seem so suitable for complexity?

One answer is the anthropic principle: We observe a universe compatible with life because otherwise we would not exist to observe it.

But cosmological natural selection gives a different possibility.

Perhaps the universe was not selected for life.

Perhaps it was selected for black holes.

Life might simply be a side effect.

Why?

The conditions that help create black holes also require complex astrophysics: stars → nuclear fusion → heavy elements → supernovae → black holes Those same stars also create the carbon, oxygen, iron, and other elements needed for planets and life.

So perhaps: The universe was not “designed” for us at all.

We may simply benefit from physical conditions that were good at producing stars and black holes.

Life could be an accidental passenger inside a universe optimized for something completely different.

Reading

Part 8: A cosmic family tree

If this process happened repeatedly, reality might contain a gigantic family tree of universes.

Imagine: Universe 1 ↓ 1,000 black holes ↓ 1,000 child universes ↓ each produces thousands of black holes ↓ millions of grandchildren universes After enough generations, the number could become enormous.

Some branches would die quickly because their physics produces almost no black holes.

Other branches would reproduce extremely successfully.

The multiverse would therefore not be a random collection of universes.

It could have: • ancestry • generations • inheritance • variation • selection In other words: The multiverse could have a history.

Just as every human belongs to an enormous biological family tree, our universe might belong to a cosmic family tree stretching through realities we can never directly observe.

Reading

Part 9: Black holes become something completely different

This hypothesis also changes the meaning of a black hole.

Normally, black holes represent destruction.

Matter falls inside.

Stars disappear.

Information seems trapped.

They are often described as cosmic graves.

But under the baby-universe idea, a black hole could simultaneously be: death from one perspective and: birth from another.

A collapsing star in our universe could produce a Big Bang somewhere else.

This creates a beautiful symmetry: Star dies → black hole forms → new universe begins → new stars form → new black holes form → more universes begin Destruction becomes reproduction.

The objects we call the “dead ends” of spacetime could actually be its reproductive organs.

That is perhaps the wildest part of the idea.

Reading

Part 10: Could our Big Bang have been a black hole?

Now reverse the idea.

If black holes in our universe create baby universes, perhaps our universe is also a baby universe.

Then somewhere in a parent cosmos, billions of years—or perhaps a completely different kind of time—ago, a star or other enormous structure may have collapsed.

A black hole formed.

From the parent's perspective: matter disappeared behind an event horizon.

From our perspective: spacetime began expanding.

Our Big Bang could therefore be the inside view of something that looked like a black hole from outside.

If true, asking: “What happened before the Big Bang?”

might be similar to asking: “What happened in the parent universe?”

But there is a serious difficulty.

The causal structure of a black hole may prevent information from the parent universe from reaching us.

We might literally be unable to look backward beyond our own cosmic birth.

Reading

Part 11: The biggest problem: where is the evidence?

This is where we must separate fascinating physics from established physics.

We know black holes exist.

We have strong astronomical evidence for them, including gravitational-wave detections and images of black-hole environments.

But we do not know that black holes create universes.

That requires physics beyond our currently confirmed understanding of black-hole interiors.

Smolin tried to make his theory scientifically useful by proposing a prediction.

If universes have evolved to maximize black-hole production, then the physical constants in our universe should be close to values that produce unusually many black holes.

If scientists could change one constant slightly in a theoretical model and reliably produce more black holes, that could challenge the hypothesis.

This makes the proposal more interesting than simply saying: “Maybe other universes exist.”

It tries to connect the idea to things we can calculate about our universe.

However, scientists continue to debate whether these tests are strong enough and whether the biological natural-selection analogy really works.

Reading

Part 12: Why the idea remains scientifically interesting

Cosmological natural selection is not the standard accepted explanation of our universe.

But the broader questions behind it remain active in theoretical physics.

Researchers continue to study: • black-hole interiors • quantum gravity • singularity removal • cosmological bounces • wormholes • baby universes Even in 2026, theoretical papers continue exploring mathematical models where baby universes can emerge from black-hole interiors or early-universe processes.

This does not mean Smolin's full theory has been confirmed.

It means the deeper question— Can one region of spacetime produce another expanding universe?

—remains a serious theoretical question.

Reading

Part 13: The deepest philosophical idea

The most powerful part of this hypothesis may not even be the black holes.

It is the idea that we might be thinking about the laws of nature incorrectly.

We usually imagine: laws first → universe follows laws But cosmological natural selection suggests: universes reproduce → laws vary → some laws reproduce more successfully Now the laws themselves become part of history.

This is similar to what Darwin did to biology.

Before Darwin, species seemed fixed.

A tiger was simply a tiger.

After Darwin, a tiger became the current result of a historical process.

Smolin asks whether we could make the same conceptual change in physics.

Perhaps an electron's mass or gravity's strength is not simply: “the number nature chose.”

Perhaps it is: the surviving result of a cosmic evolutionary history.

Whether this is true or not, that question completely changes how we think about the universe.
